questions.title: What is the difference between Interfaces and Type Aliases in TypeScript?
questions.description:
Interface vs. Type Alias

Both interfaces and type aliases can be used to describe the shape of an object or a function signature, but they differ in capabilities and intent.

Differences

  • Declaration Merging: Interfaces support declaration merging (you can define the same interface multiple times and they will merge). Types do not.
  • Unions and Primitives: Type aliases can represent primitives, unions, tuples, and intersections. Interfaces are strictly for object structures.
  • Extending: Interfaces extend other interfaces/classes using the extends keyword. Types extend using intersections (&).
questions.bestPractices:
• Use interface for object shapes where public extension/merging might be useful (like library APIs).
  • Use type for unions, tuples, mapping types, or complex conditional signatures.
questions.commonMistakes: • Trying to redefine a type alias which throws a duplicate identifier error.
questions.example:
// Interface Merging
interface User {
  name: string;
}
interface User {
  age: number;
}
const user: User = { name: 'Dev', age: 25 }; // Merged!

// Type Union
type AuthState = 'logged-in' | 'logged-out';
// Interfaces cannot do this directly!
questions.interviewTip: Summarize: 'Use interfaces by default for standard object API descriptions. Use types when you need unions, tuples, or complex operations.'
